title: Radical Numerics creates first AI-generated phages to reach human patient
content:
Radical Numerics creates first AI-generated phages to reach human patient with Omnii-1
Antibiotic resistance is a growing global concern, projected to cause approximately 40 million deaths over the next 25 years1. Phage therapy offers a promising alternative when antibiotics fail, but finding phages that target a patient’s bacterial infection remains a major challenge. We trained Omnii-1, our multimodal genome language model, to help bridge this gap. We demonstrate that it can generate viable phages, prioritize variants, and predict phage-host interactions. In the world's first clinical use of AI-generated phages, Omnii-1 designs were administered to a human patient under compassionate use, marking a milestone toward personalized, AI-designed therapies for antibiotic-resistant infections.
Antibiotics have transformed medicine, making once-fatal bacterial infections routinely treatable. But bacteria evolve, developing resistance through mutations and the acquisition of resistance genes. Multidrug-resistant bacteria are increasingly making antibiotics less effective. In 2021, antibiotic resistance was associated with an estimated 4.7 million deaths worldwide. Between 2025 and 2050, deaths attributable to antibiotic resistance are projected to total nearly 40 million1.
One promising solution to this crisis comes from bacteria's natural enemies: phages. These viruses are found in all microbial ecosystems, from oceans and soil to the human gut2,3. They have evolved alongside bacteria for billions of years, developing mechanisms to recognize and infect particular bacterial hosts. During a lyticaa Lytic phages reproduce inside bacteria and destroy them without entering a dormant phase. They are generally preferred for phage therapy over temperate phages, which can establish lysogeny4. phage infection, a phage attaches to a susceptible bacterium, delivers its genetic material, and replicates inside the cell. Eventually, the cell bursts, killing the bacterium and releasing new phages that can infect other bacteria.
The idea behind phage therapy is deceptively simple: find phages that can kill the bacteria causing a patient's infection and administer them as a treatment. Phages do not infect human cells, and phage therapy is generally considered safe4. Unlike broad-spectrum antibiotics, phages can target particular bacteria with remarkable specificity, sparing beneficial bacteria such as those in the gut that support digestion. This specificity is both the promise and the challenge of phage therapy: treatments can be highly targeted, but suitable phages must be found or designed for each infection.
Today, personalized phage therapy largely depends on empirical search, as the biological mechanisms governing phage-host specificity are not yet fully understood for many clinically relevant pathogens. Starting with a bacterial sample from a patient's infection, researchers screen existing phage collections for effective candidates, turning to additional collections, environmental samples, or engineering when none are suitable5,6. For patients with severe infections and few remaining options, these delays can be life-threatening. We need efficient ways to develop personalized phage therapies for patients who cannot afford to wait.
Our goal at Radical Numerics is to use artificial intelligence (AI) to understand and engineer biology, enabling new approaches to therapeutic design. To bridge this gap in effective phage therapy, we trained Omnii-1, our multimodal genome language model, to help identify and design phages that target specific bacterial strains. We aim to use these capabilities to develop suitable phage therapies for patients whose infections have few remaining treatment options.
Making phage therapy accessible to more patients will require robust workflows for designing effective phages against individual infections. Here, we describe our approach and the challenges that remain.
Building a personalized phage therapy
Developing a personalized phage therapy begins with a bacterial isolate: a sample of the bacteria causing a patient's infection. The goal is to find or design phages that kill the target bacteria. Understanding the genetic features that shape a phage's specificity for particular bacterial strains is central to this challenge.
What determines a phage’s ability to infect a bacterium?
Phage infection begins with molecular recognition. A phage must first attach to a compatible receptor on the bacterial surface, often with high specificity. These receptors can include proteins, lipopolysaccharides, capsules, and pili. Small differences in receptor structure can allow a phage to recognize one bacterial strain but not another.
However, recognition is only the first challenge. After attachment, a phage must deliver its genome, overcome bacterial defensesbb For example, restriction-modification systems cut phage DNA lacking protective methylation, while CRISPR-Cas systems use RNA guides to target matching sequences. Phages can counter these defenses through DNA modifications or proteins that inhibit these systems., and replicate inside the cell to produce new phages (Figure 2). Failure at any of these steps can prevent a phage from establishing a productive infection, even after successfully recognizing a bacterium.
These interactions make phage engineering a challenging biological design problem. Changes to a phage's genome can alter which bacteria it recognizes but may also disrupt functions required for assembly or replication. Successful engineering requires improving activity against the target bacteria while preserving the machinery necessary for infection.
From phage discovery to phage design
Researchers traditionally begin developing phage therapies by screening collections of naturally occurring phages against a patient's bacterial isolate. When suitable candidates are unavailable, engineering phage variants offers another possibility. Previous clinical applications have included engineered phages modified to promote lytic infection or equipped with CRISPR systems to enhance antibacterial activity5,6.
Similarly, using AI to generate new phage variants does not require designing an entirely new genome. Instead, we can modify selected regions involved in particular biological functions. For example, receptor-binding proteins help determine which bacterial strains a phage can recognize by binding to specific receptors on the bacterial surface, making them promising targets for engineering host specificity. By changing the DNA encoding these proteins, we can explore new patterns of host recognition while preserving the broader phage genome.
Still, even a short DNA region has an enormous number of possible sequencescc A region of n nucleotides has 4ⁿ possible DNA sequences., only a fraction of which may preserve phage function. Exploring this sequence space through random mutations and experimental screening alone is resource intensive at scale. Genome language models offer a way to generate promising variants, guide designs toward specific bacterial targets, and prioritize them for experimental testing.
How Omnii-1 designs phages
Recent advances in machine learning have demonstrated complementary capabilities for phage genome design and phage-host interaction prediction. King et al. showed that Evo, a genome language model, could generate viable ΦX174-like bacteriophages (hereafter “EvoPhage”)7. Separately, Gaborieau et al. and subsequent studies demonstrated strain-level phage-host prediction from genomic information using machine learning methods8,9,10,11.
Our goal is to build on these capabilities to design phages with therapeutic activity against specific bacterial strains.
Learning the language of phage genomes
Omnii-1 is pretrained on diverse genomic sequences and multiomics data, then further trained on phage genomes to adapt its knowledge to these biological systems.

report.summary: Radical Numerics says its Omnii-1 genome language model generated viable phages that were given to a patient under compassionate use, a first for AI-designed phage therapy.
report.background: Antibiotic resistance is a escalating global health crisis: in 2021 it was associated with an estimated 4.7 million deaths, and deaths attributable to resistance are projected to total nearly 40 million between 2025 and 2050. Phage therapy, which uses bacteria-killing viruses, offers a targeted alternative when antibiotics fail, but finding suitable phages is slow and largely empirical. Clinicians screen phage collections, environmental samples, and engineered variants against a patient's bacterial isolate, and delays can be life-threatening. AI genome language models are emerging as a way to generate and prioritize phage variants and predict phage-host interactions. Radical Numerics trained Omnii-1, a multimodal genome language model, on diverse genomic and multiomics data and then phage genomes to design phages for specific bacterial strains.
key_points: Radical Numerics reports the first clinical use of AI-generated phages: Omnii-1-designed phages were administered to a human patient under compassionate use. The company frames this as a milestone toward personalized, AI-designed therapies for antibiotic-resistant infections, though it is a single compassionate-use case rather than a controlled trial.

Omnii-1 is a multimodal genome language model trained on diverse genomic and multiomics data, then adapted to phage genomes. Radical Numerics says it can generate viable phages, prioritize variants for testing, and predict phage-host interactions. The approach can modify targeted regions such as receptor-binding proteins rather than redesigning an entire phage genome.

Phage design is biologically difficult because infection requires receptor recognition, genome delivery, overcoming bacterial defenses, and replication. A change that improves host recognition can break assembly or replication, and even short DNA regions have enormous sequence space. AI helps generate and rank promising variants, reducing reliance on random mutation and large experimental screens.

The work builds on prior research: Evo, a genome language model, generated viable ΦX174-like phages, and separate machine-learning methods have predicted strain-level phage-host interactions. Radical Numerics aims to go further by designing phages with therapeutic activity against specific bacterial strains; the article cites engineered T7 as one example of its Omnii-1 work.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the case is a high-profile validation that genome language models can move from sequence generation to clinically relevant biological design. It will increase attention on wet-lab validation, biosafety, regulatory pathways, and benchmarks for AI-generated therapeutics. For developers, the key challenges are host-range prediction, variant prioritization, and proving that designs are viable and safe, not just plausible sequences. For patients, the hope is faster personalized phage therapy when antibiotics fail, but a compassionate-use case does not demonstrate efficacy. Access, cost, manufacturing, and regulatory acceptance will determine whether AI-designed phages become routine rather than exceptional.
report.tools: Watch Radical Numerics' Omnii-1, Arc Institute's Evo genome language model, and open-source tools such as PhageAI for phage biology prediction. Also follow phage-host interaction benchmarks from Gaborieau et al. and related machine-learning studies. For experimental follow-up, standard phage isolation, host-range assays, and compassionate-use regulatory frameworks remain essential; AI models are decision-support and design tools, not substitutes for wet-lab validation.
